claims.newSentence: Blood in the urine is the most common sign of bladder cancer, according to Macmillan and MedlinePlus. Many people with blood in their urine do not have bladder cancer, but the NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111. Smoking is the biggest known risk factor for bladder cancer. Treatment depends on the stage and type of the cancer, and the NHS says surgery is usually offered first, with chemotherapy, radiotherapy or immunotherapy added in some cases.

claims.newSentence: A GP usually sees a person first and may ask for a urine sample to be sent for testing. The sample is checked for infection and, in some cases, for cancer cells. If the GP thinks cancer is possible or is unsure of the cause, they refer the person to a urologist, a specialist in the urinary tract. The main test is a cystoscopy, in which a thin camera is passed through the urethra to look inside the bladder. Imaging such as a CT urogram may also be used, and abnormal areas can be removed in an operation called TURBT so they can be tested for cancer.

claims.newSentence: Treatment depends on the stage and type of the cancer. The NHS says surgery is usually offered first, and chemotherapy, radiotherapy, targeted medicines or immunotherapy may be added depending on the case. For early-stage disease, treatments such as BCG or mitomycin can be placed directly into the bladder. Removing the whole bladder, called cystectomy, is used for higher-risk or muscle-invasive disease, and radiotherapy with chemotherapy is another approach.

notes: Second pass used 11 WebSearch calls, all domain-restricted with differently worded queries. Tool summaries blend pages; attributions marked 'via search summary' are not page-certain. The old NHS URL /diagnosis/ was not returned; the real page is /tests-and-next-steps/ (title only seen) and was kept only as a supporting reference in the ledger. Cut: NHS 'more than a third' now attributed to NHS 111 Wales with Macmillan 'about half'; 'painless', chewing tobacco, catheter, radiotherapy, overweight, diabetes, relative, kidney-function/blood-count tests, NCI diagnosis sentence, cystectomy quality-of-life claim, PMC10369196/PMC10800852 claims (not re-retrieved; replaced with retrieved reviews PMC8571151, PMC12327299, PMC12647504, PMC12282301, PMC5433354, PMC4779141). Route to care reworded to NHS wording: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 (no 999 claim retrieved). tests list trimmed to urinalysis and biopsy. Recurrence and BCG statements rest on PMC reviews seen only as search summaries; Macmillan 'about half' came from an unnamed Macmillan page in a summary. Human reviewer should glance at the urologist-referral and 'stage, grade and type' removal choices.
